SECTION 7.1

Properties of the
normal distribution.

Use a uniform model, recognize a normal curve, state its properties, and explain probability as area.

1. A uniform probability distribution

In the delivery example, X measures minutes after 10 a.m., with possible times from 0 to 60. Any two equal-length intervals within the hour have equal probabilities.

Density height = 160
Total area = 60 × 160 = 1

The density is zero outside the interval from 0 to 60. For an interval inside that hour, multiply its width by the density height.

Work the notes' 15-to-30-minute example
P(15 ≤ X ≤ 30) = (30 − 15) × 160 = 1560 = 0.2500

The probability of delivery between 10:15 and 10:30 is 0.25.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, pages 2–7.

2. Two requirements for a density function

Total area equals 1.

Across all possible values of the continuous random variable, the entire area under the graph is 1.

Density is never negative.

The graph's height is greater than or equal to zero for every possible value.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, page 3.

3. Recognize and describe a normal curve

A normal relative-frequency histogram is bell-shaped and symmetric. The normal density curve has these properties:

  1. It is symmetric about the mean, μ.
  2. Mean = median = mode. Its single highest point occurs at x = μ.
  3. Inflection points occur at μ − σ and μ + σ.
  4. Total area under the curve is 1.
  5. Half the area is to the left of μ and half is to the right.
  6. Both tails approach, but never reach, the horizontal axis.
  7. The Empirical Rule gives the approximate areas within one, two, and three standard deviations.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, pages 8–12.

4. The Empirical Rule

Select a band to shade the approximate area within that number of standard deviations of the mean.

These are the approximate percentages stated in the notes. They are not rounded versions of the more precise numerical areas used in Section 7.2.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, pages 12–13.

5. Build the height histogram

The notes list heights, in inches, of 50 two-year-old males. Use a first lower class limit of 31.5 and class width 1. Select a bar to connect its relative frequency with area.

Select a class interval in the histogram.

See the 50 heights from the notes

Each bar's area is its observed proportion because the class width is 1. The normal curve in the notes provides a smooth approximation; the sample histogram and a model need not match exactly.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, pages 14–18.

6. Give area two interpretations

Giraffe weights are approximately normal with μ = 2,200 pounds and σ = 200 pounds. The notes give an area of 0.3085 to the left of 2,100 pounds.

Population proportion

The proportion of giraffes weighing less than 2,100 pounds is 0.3085.

Individual probability

The probability that a randomly selected giraffe weighs less than 2,100 pounds is 0.3085.

Source: Section 7.1 notes, pages 19–21.

SECTION 7.2

Find the area.
Then find the value.

Standardize a normal variable, use left-tail areas, and reverse the process to find a percentile or a middle interval.

1. Standardize a normal variable

Z = X − μσ
Standard normal distribution: mean 0, standard deviation 1.

For the IQ example, μ = 100 and σ = 15. An IQ score of 120 has z = 120 − 10015 ≈ 1.33. The score is about 1.33 standard deviations above the mean.

Connect z = 1.33 to the table and the complement

Table V gives P(Z < 1.33) = 0.9082. The area to the right is 1 − 0.9082 = 0.0918.

These use the rounded z-score 1.33, following the slides. Direct numerical calculation at x = 120 gives a slightly different result.

Source: Section 7.2 notes, pages 2–7.

For an X value, first compute z = x − μσ. For an interval, standardize both endpoints before subtracting the left-tail areas.

3. Read a left-tail standard normal table

The table gives the area to the left of a z-score. The row supplies its tenths and the column supplies its hundredths. For z = 1.33, use row 1.3 and column 0.03.

This small table excerpt is computed from the standard normal model to reproduce the four-decimal left-tail entries used in the notes.

Source: Section 7.2 notes, pages 4, 6, 9, 11–12.

4. Find an X value from an area

  1. Draw a normal curve and shade the area described by the proportion, probability, or percentile.
  2. Find the corresponding z-score in Table V.
  3. Use x = μ + zσ.
x = μ + zσ

GRE: 85th percentile

Using the GRE example exactly as presented in the notes, μ = 1,049 and σ = 189. The left-tail area is 0.85 and the notes use z = 1.04.

x = 1,049 + 1.04(189) = 1,245.56 ≈ 1,246.

A score of about 1,246 is at the 85th percentile in this model.

Steel rods: middle 90%

μ = 100 cm, σ = 0.45 cm. Split the remaining 10% into two 5% tails. The notes use z₁ = −1.645 and z₂ = 1.645.

x₁ = 100 − 1.645(0.45) ≈ 99.26 cm.
x₂ = 100 + 1.645(0.45) ≈ 100.74 cm.

Source: Section 7.2 notes, pages 16–20. The GRE example is reproduced as given; it is not a statement about a current test scale.

5. Explore percentiles and middle intervals

Source: Section 7.2 notes, pages 16–20.

6. Read zα correctly

zα is the z-score with area α to its right. To use a left-tail table, look for area 1 − α.

P(Z > zα) = α
Left-tail area = 1 − α

In the steel-rod example, a right-tail area of 0.05 corresponds to z ≈ 1.645. The lower cutoff is its negative.

Source: Section 7.2 notes, pages 20–21.

7.2 · COMPUTE WITH R

Normal probabilities and percentiles in R

Open Posit Cloud ↗

Open an RStudio project in Posit Cloud and paste the code into the Console. No additional packages are needed. Use pnorm() for an area or probability and qnorm() to find a value from a left-tail probability. A z-score is computed with (x - mu) / sigma.

TaskR expressionMeaning
Left tailpnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)P(X < x)
Right tailpnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)P(X > x)
Between two valuespnorm(b, mu, sigma) - pnorm(a, mu, sigma)P(a < X < b)
Percentileqnorm(p, mean = mu, sd = sigma)The value with proportion p below it; enter 45% as 0.45.

In these templates, replace x, a, b, mu, and sigma with the problem's values, or assign those variables first.

Examples with unrounded calculations

# X is normal with mean 70 and standard deviation 8
# Left tail: P(X < 80)
pnorm(80, mean = 70, sd = 8)

# Right tail: P(X > 80)
pnorm(80, mean = 70, sd = 8, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Interval: P(65 < X < 80)
pnorm(80, 70, 8) - pnorm(65, 70, 8)

# 40th percentile
qnorm(0.40, mean = 70, sd = 8)

Match the method requested in the workshop

Direct R calls use unrounded values. Some supplied multiple-choice answers use z-scores rounded to two decimals and table probabilities rounded to four decimals. These methods can give slightly different answers. The code leaves results unrounded. Apply the rounding instructions yourself; when an intermediate z-score must be rounded, run that line first and replace z with your rounded value before continuing. For a percentile, rounding z before converting back to x also changes the result.

# Percentile calculation: apply the stated rounding yourself
z <- qnorm(0.40)
70 + z * 8

# Right-tail calculation: apply the stated rounding yourself
z <- (445 - 349) / 72
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)

dnorm() returns density height, not a cumulative probability. R guidance: R normal-distribution documentation ↗.
